changes.after: Use the fresh iterator returned after removing a vector item.

before: A vector operation can invalidate iterators, references and pointers into its elements. Reallocation during growth invalidates all of them. erase invalidates positions at and after the erased element.
vector::erase returns a fresh iterator to the element following the erased one, or end if there is none. Replace the old iterator with that result and check end before dereferencing.
Using an invalidated iterator is not a reliable way to see an old value; it can be undefined behavior. This example only reads the newly returned valid position.

Expected output or behavior: 4
. Local compiler test evidence is recorded separately from app reading completion.

Optional local transfer task: Build an erase-while-iterating loop that removes even values, always using erase’s returned iterator. You may trace this without a compiler; finishing the reading is not proof of a local run.
after: Invalidate means make something no longer valid to use in its old way. Erasing a vector item invalidates iterators and references at that position and after it. Do not keep using the old position to read an item.
erase returns a fresh iterator to the following item. If no following item exists, it returns the vector's new end position. Assign that result back to position.
The returned iterator may be end(), so compare before reading *position. This handles removing the last remaining item too.
The program prints 4. Erasing the first item removes two. The returned iterator identifies the following item, four, which is now first.

Growing a vector can move its items to new storage. When that reallocation happens, all old iterators, references, and pointers into its items become invalid. Use each operation's rules before keeping a saved position.

before.question: Use a vector containing only 2, then erase it. What prints?
choices: end, because erase returns the new end position
before.explanation: After erasing the sole element the vector is empty. The returned iterator equals end, so the guard selects the end branch.

after.question: Start with a vector containing only 2, then erase it. What prints?
choices: end, because erase returns the empty vector's end position.
after.explanation: No item remains after the removal. The check detects end() and avoids reading an item.
